entry.title: Agentic TCAD Calibration: From the Paper to a Reproducible Open Demo

link.title: Agentic TCAD Calibration: From the Paper to a Reproducible Open Demo

entry.content:
Paper: Agentic TCAD Calibration Workflow for Oxide Semiconductor Transistors (arXiv:2609.12184)
Demo Code: github.com/gyulab/agentic-TCAD-calibration-public

This work is a collaboration between Georgia Tech, Samsung Electronics, and NVIDIA.

Disclaimer: This educational post and the demo are not affiliated with or endorsed by Synopsys, Inc. No Synopsys software, documentation, license, input deck, or proprietary example is distributed. The demo uses synthetic data and does not reproduce the paper’s measured-device or Sentaurus results.


Motivation: calibration is an inverse problem

    TCAD calibration is essential for predictive modeling of emerging oxide-semiconductor transistors. It is also slow and expert dependent. Several physical models and parameter sets can reproduce the same measured transfer curve, so a good local fit does not identify the underlying device physics. An engineer therefore spends most of the time deciding what to try next: which parameter to move, how far, and when an extra physics model is justified.

    Our paper turns these decisions into an explicit, auditable loop. Measurement–TCAD residuals and local sensitivity tests choose the next bounded update. An update is accepted only if the simulation converges and a fixed device objective improves. The point is to make each step of the calibration reviewable, so the final model can be trusted beyond the curve it was fitted to.


The workflow in the paper

    The paper calibrates a fabricated bottom-gate In–W–O (BG-IWO) transistor with Synopsys Sentaurus. Three roles are kept separate:

Role Responsibility
LLM agent Analyze residuals and device metrics, retrieve evidence (RAG), and propose a bounded TCAD update
TCAD simulator Solve the device equations and return the transfer curve and convergence status
Human reviewer Define the device stack and test splits, approve model changes, and check physical validity


    Each update is scored with a multi-metric objective J. J combines log- and linear-current errors with the errors in Vth (at 100 nA), log Ion, and subthreshold swing (SS). One-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) probes estimate the local sensitivity of each parameter group. A bounded, derivative-free Gauss–Newton (DFO-GN) step then proposes the change. An additional physics model, such as a fixed charge or a Gaussian/tail density of states, is considered only when a systematic residual persists after the existing parameters have been adjusted.

    In the paper, five accepted updates reduce J from 2.589 to 0.181 (14.3×). The calibrated model is then held fixed. Maximum Vth/Ion errors are 36.1 mV/0.022 dec for varying drain bias and 46.2 mV/0.062 dec for varying channel length. These held-out tests are what separate a transferable model from a local curve fit.


Why an open demo

    The paper’s results depend on measured device data, calibrated Sentaurus decks, and a commercial license. None of these can be shared. A reader who wants to see how the loop actually makes decisions would therefore have nothing to run.

    The open demo keeps the workflow and replaces everything proprietary. A small analytic transistor model stands in for Sentaurus, and synthetic curves stand in for the measurement. The demo needs only Python with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, and PyYAML, and it finishes in about 5 s on a laptop CPU. It demonstrates the decision logic, not the device physics of In–W–O.


A synthetic device with known missing physics

    The simulator is a charge-based (EKV-style) transfer-curve model with a Schottky-like contact resistance solved self-consistently. It depends on gate voltage, drain bias, and channel length. That dependence matters, because a held-out test on a model that ignores L would be meaningless. The calibration parameters mirror the paper’s effective descriptors: S/D work function (contact), gate work function, mobility prefactor μ0, and two optional components, a gate-interface fixed charge Qf and a tail-state density Ntail.

    The synthetic “measurement” is generated by the same model plus two effects that the calibration model never has: a gate-dependent mobility and a drain-induced threshold shift. Noise and a pA-level floor are added with a fixed seed. A perfect fit is therefore impossible by construction. This avoids the “inverse crime” of fitting data with the model that generated it, and it gives the held-out tests real model-form error to reveal.


Objective J and the accept rule

    The demo uses the paper’s objective (Eq. 1) with the same weights and metric windows:

\[J=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{cal}|}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{cal}}\Big[0.25\,E_{\log,b}+0.10\,E_{\mathrm{lin},b}+1.00\,|\Delta V_{th,b}|+0.20\,|\Delta\log_{10}I_{on,b}|+0.25\,|\Delta SS_b|\Big]\]

    The calibration biases are VD = 0.05 and 1 V at L = 1 µm. The paper states that each term is normalized by a fixed factor but does not list the values. The demo therefore declares its own normalization in the config, so its J values cannot be compared with the paper’s.

    The bounded update solves the paper’s Eq. (3): a weighted least-squares step inside the parameter box and a trust radius. The rule that follows is strict. A trial is accepted only if every calibration simulation converges and J decreases. Otherwise it is rejected, logged with its reason, and retried with a smaller step. This rule is what keeps an automated loop from drifting into a better-looking but unphysical fit.


Agent and optimizer are different things

    The most important design choice is the split between choosing and computing. The planner only chooses among legal actions: update one parameter group, request a model activation, or stop. The numbers always come from the OFAT and Gauss–Newton tools, and the accept rule is enforced by the controller. A planner can therefore never bypass the bounds or the objective, however it is implemented.

    The default planner is a deterministic, rule-based controller. It is not an LLM. It activates a component that addresses the dominant residual when one is eligible. Otherwise it updates the group with the largest predicted gain, and it stops when nothing legal remains. An optional LLM planner can be connected to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. It receives the same observation as JSON and must return one legal action. Invalid output is logged as an error, and the run never silently falls back to the rule planner. The default path thus needs no API key, while a real LLM can be plugged in without changing the guard rails.

    Every decision is written to an action log, one JSON line per event:

{"event": "trial", "group": "contact", "changes": {"phi_SD": {"from": 4.75, "to": 4.51}},
 "J_before": 13.61, "J_trial": 11.40, "decision": "accepted", "reason": "converged and J decreased"}

    A reviewer can replay the whole calibration from this log and check why each step was taken.


Residual-guided model activation

    Adding physics is the riskiest decision in calibration, because almost any extra term lowers the error. The demo therefore makes a component eligible only under three conditions. Its residual must carry at least 15% of J. It must persist through bounded parameter updates. And a trigger must show that existing parameters cannot remove it. Even then the activation needs an approval record, either from a policy file or from the researcher at the terminal.

    Two triggers appear in the default run. The gate work function reaches its approved bound while a Vth offset remains, so the workflow requests the fixed charge Qf. Later, the SS residual persists while no active parameter can move it to first order, so the workflow requests the tail-state term. Because both candidates share the synthetic truth’s functional forms, the meaningful check is the negative one. When the synthetic device lacks a component, the workflow does not activate it. This selectivity is tested directly, and it is the evidence that the gate is not trivially permissive.


Results on synthetic data

    The run starts from a deliberately poor model with a high contact barrier, a Vth offset of about 0.7 V, and no tail states.


    The workflow first moves the gate work function to its bound, then corrects the contact and mobility, and then activates Qf and the tail-state term when their residuals persist. J falls from 20.77 to 0.407 over 17 accepted updates, with 6 rejected trials. Parameter tuning alone stalls near J = 8.5. The largest single drop, from 8.49 to 2.66, comes with the fixed-charge activation. After the tail-state activation, J falls by another factor of four within four updates. The added terms therefore appear to remove systematic errors that the original parameters could not reach.


    The residual breakdown explains each action. Once the Vth offset is corrected, the SS share of J grows from below 10% to about 40%. That persistent share is what triggers the tail-state activation. It falls to about 4% once the tail-state density has been adjusted.



    Not every parameter is identified. The gate work function and Qf enter only through VT, so only their combination is fixed by the data. μ0 also absorbs the gate-dependent mobility that the model lacks. The contact work function and the tail-state density are recovered closely. This mirrors the paper’s caution that fitted values are calibration-effective descriptors, not physical extractions.


Held-out evaluation without retuning

    The calibrated model is then held fixed and evaluated on conditions it never saw: VD = 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5 V at L = 1 µm, and L = 2 µm at both calibration biases. A test confirms that corrupting the held-out data leaves the calibration unchanged.

Condition max |ΔVth| max |Δlog Ion|
Calibration (L = 1 µm, VD = 0.05, 1 V) 16.9 mV 0.031 dec
Held-out drain bias (VD = 0.1–0.5 V) 16.9 mV 0.024 dec
Held-out channel length (L = 2 µm) 17.0 mV 0.021 dec



    The remaining Vth errors are model-form error, not noise. They stay at 14–19 mV with the noise switched off, and they fall to about 3 mV when the missing physics is removed from the synthetic device. The held-out drain biases lie between the two calibration biases, so that test is an interpolation in VD, while the L = 2 µm test changes the geometry. Across ten noise seeds, final J ranges from 0.34 to 0.43 and the held-out Vth error from 17 to 23 mV, so the seed shown here is on the favorable side.


Run it yourself

git clone https://github.com/gyulab/agentic-TCAD-calibration-public
cd agentic-TCAD-calibration-public
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-lock.txt && pip install -e . --no-deps
python -m agentic_tcad_demo run --config configs/synthetic_demo.yaml
pytest

    The run writes the action log, a summary with the J trajectory and held-out tables, the final parameters, and the five figures above. Two runs give byte-identical outputs. --interactive asks the researcher before each model activation, and --planner llm connects an LLM through environment variables. A private simulator, such as an in-house TCAD wrapper, can be plugged in through a small Simulator interface without adding any deck or license file to the repository.


What the demo does not show

    The demo has clear limits, and they are worth stating once. It does not implement RAG. Retrieval from the Sentaurus manual cannot be redistributed, so candidate components are listed in the config instead. The optional LLM planner has not yet been evaluated with a specific model. The compact model is a teaching instrument, so a good synthetic calibration says nothing about industrial TCAD accuracy. Finally, the paper’s numbers come from measured data and Sentaurus, and they cannot be reproduced without those assets.


Takeaway

    An agentic calibration workflow is useful less for its speed than for its discipline. Residuals decide what to probe. Updates stay inside approved bounds. New physics needs evidence and approval, and every step must improve a fixed objective. Held-out conditions then test whether the model transfers. The open demo makes this discipline concrete enough to run, inspect, and test, and the same pattern would apply to other inverse problems with expensive simulators.


Related: An earlier practical guide on setting up coding agents for generic TCAD tasks (AGENTS.md, SKILL.md, local manual search, and execution gates) is available as a PDF.
entry.summary: A residual-guided, bounded, tool-using workflow for TCAD calibration of oxide-semiconductor transistors, with an open synthetic-data demo that runs on a laptop without a TCAD license.

entry.title: IRPS 2026: PINN-Assisted Compact Modeling for nvCAP Arrays

link.title: IRPS 2026: PINN-Assisted Compact Modeling for nvCAP Arrays

entry.content:
Paper (IRPS 2026): Physics-Informed Neural Network-Assisted Compact Modeling for Process Variation in Non-volatile Capacitive Crossbar Arrays (IEEE Xplore)
Authors: Gyujun Jeong, Jungyoun Kwak, Madhav Vadlamani, Junmo Lee, and Shimeng Yu (Georgia Tech)
All paper figures in this post are © 2026 IEEE, reprinted with permission.

IRPS (International Reliability Physics Symposium) 2026 was my first time presenting at a conference! I presented how custom physics-informed loss functions can guide neural network compact models to stay physically consistent, here applied to process variation (PV) in ferroelectric non-volatile capacitor (nvCAP) crossbar arrays.



Motivation: Process Variation in Scaled nvCAP

    The ferroelectric nvCAP is a promising device for non-destructive read and charge-domain compute-in-memory. So far, nvCAP data have mostly been measured at the µm scale, but as devices shrink to the nm regime, stochastic fabrication variations—ferroelectric thickness, dielectric constant, work function—can cause large deviations in device characteristics. Projecting yield and accuracy at future nodes requires a predictive PV-aware compact model.

Each compact modeling approach has a trade-off:

Modeling Method Advantages Limitations
Physics-based Model (TCAD) High physical fidelity; captures internal states Computationally expensive; effort-intensive calibration
Data-driven Model (MLP) Fast inference; simple implementation Physical inconsistency; risk of unphysical oscillations
PINN Model (This work) Physics-aware accuracy; robust generalization Requires custom loss function design


    Neural network compact models offer > 105× inference speedup over physics-based solvers, but a pure black box can violate physical laws between training points. Our goal is to keep the speed of an MLP while forcing it to respect the physics.


PINN compact modeling framework: TCAD C-V data under PV → PINN-assisted compact model → SPICE → ENOB of a 128×128 nvCAP crossbar.



Device and TCAD Data Under Process Variation

    We study a 3D fin nvCAP with an ALD-grown W-doped In2O3 (IWO) oxide semiconductor layer in series with a ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) layer. The capacitance is high (Con) when the IWO is accumulated and low (Coff) when it is depleted, and the ferroelectric polarization sets which state is read at Vread = 0 V.


Since statistical variation data at these dimensions do not exist yet, we used an experimentally calibrated Sentaurus TCAD nvCAP model to synthesize C-V data over three process corners:

Sweep Parameter Default Value Variation (3 Process Corners)
HZO Dielectric Constant (εHZO) 14 Nominal ± 10%: {12.6, 14, 15.4}
HZO Thickness (tHZO) 7 nm Nominal ± 10%: {6.3, 7, 7.7} nm
Bottom Electrode Work Function (WF) 4.5 eV Nominal ± 0.1 eV: {4.4, 4.5, 4.6} eV
Overlap Width (Wov) 40 nm {4, 10, 40} nm


(Default design: W = 200 nm, L = 100 nm, Lov = 25 nm)

Physical Trends (What the Model Must Respect)


  • Work function: shifts the C-V curve laterally (built-in field offset).
  • εHZO ↑ / tHZO ↓: both Con and Coff increase, since capacitance is governed by CHZO ∝ εHZO/tHZO. The on/off ratio also increases, because Con depends almost entirely on CHZO while Coff is a series combination with the depletion capacitance.
  • Wov ↓: absolute capacitance decreases (smaller overlap area), but the on/off ratio increases because Coff scales with the overlap area while Con is preserved by accumulation extending beyond the overlap.

These are exactly the monotone relationships that we later encode into the loss function.



Methodology: PINN with Monotonicity Constraints

Architecture


The compact model is a small 6-32-32-1 MLP:

  • Inputs (6): gate voltage Vg, a binary on/off branch indicator (Con vs. Coff branch of the ferroelectric hysteresis), and four PV parameters (εHZO, tHZO, WF, Wov).
  • Output (1): capacitance C.
  • Training data: ~16k points from TCAD, swept over a coarse 3-corner grid (Nominal, +10%, −10%) to emulate a realistic, data-efficient design of experiments.

Why Monotonicity?

    With only three corners per parameter, a standard MLP easily fits the training points but produces ripples and staircase artifacts in between. A small ripple may look harmless, but a non-monotonic C-V is physically wrong (capacitance must not decrease as Vg sweeps through the switching transition), and it can cause convergence failures in array-level SPICE simulation.


(a) The standard MLP (red) oscillates around the TCAD reference while the PINN (green) stays smooth. (b) The MLP gradient ∂C/∂V dips below zero (violation regions). (c) The ReLU physics loss lights up exactly at those violations.

ReLU-Based Physics Loss

The total loss combines the data fit with a weighted sum of physics penalties:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{Total} = \mathcal{L}_{MSE} + \mathcal{L}_{R} = \mathcal{L}_{MSE} + \sum_{k} \lambda_k \cdot \mathcal{L}_{Physics,k} $$


The key building block is \(ReLU(x) = \max(0, x)\), which acts as a conditional filter: it is zero when the physics is satisfied and positive only when it is violated. Using automatic differentiation, we compute the partial derivatives of the predicted capacitance with respect to the inputs during training and penalize negative C-V slopes:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{V} = ReLU\left(-\frac{\partial C}{\partial V}\right) $$


If \(\partial C / \partial V \geq 0\) (physically correct), the penalty is exactly zero; any negative slope produces a positive loss that the optimizer must remove. We extend the same idea to the process trends from TCAD, so that capacitance decreases with tHZO and increases with εHZO and Wov:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{R} = \lambda_V \cdot ReLU\left(-\frac{\partial C}{\partial V}\right) + \lambda_t \cdot ReLU\left(\frac{\partial C}{\partial t}\right) + \lambda_\varepsilon \cdot ReLU\left(-\frac{\partial C}{\partial \varepsilon}\right) + \lambda_W \cdot ReLU\left(-\frac{\partial C}{\partial W}\right) $$


with \(\lambda_V = 0.05\) and \(\lambda_t = \lambda_\varepsilon = \lambda_W = 0.01\), chosen to balance the derivative magnitudes so the physics term guides the fit without overwhelming the data term. Unlike generic regularization (e.g., weight decay), these inequality constraints create a physical boundary that guides the optimizer even in regions with no training data.

    Note) The same monotone-constraint idea later became the monotonicity loss for retention time in our PINO surrogate for Fe-VNAND (ICMC 2026), where trapped charge and remnant polarization must decay monotonically.



Results

1. Interpolation to an Unseen Process Corner


We tested both models on an unseen, experimentally calibrated εHZO = 13.5, between the trained 12.6 and 14 corners, focusing on the steep transition region (20–30 fF/µm²):

  • Standard MLP: R2 = 0.67, with unphysical oscillations.
  • PINN: R2 = 0.96, smooth and closely matching TCAD.

    Interestingly, the standard MLP had a lower training MSE (1×10-5) than the PINN (3×10-5). The lower number reflects overfitting to the sparse grid; the slightly higher PINN training loss is the expected price of the physics constraints, and it buys robust generalization.

2. Monte Carlo Variation of Con / Coff


    Monte Carlo sampling of the compact model (varying εHZO, tHZO, WF, with Wov = 4 nm to maximize the on/off ratio) shows Con spanning ~22–30 fF/µm² and Coff ~1.5–1.9 fF/µm². The relative variation is comparable for both states (~20–30%).

3. Array-Level Impact: 128×128 Capacitive Crossbar


    Plugging the PINN compact model into SPICE for a 128×128 nvCAP crossbar (charging + charge transfer phases), with thermal, jitter, and flicker noise, we computed the ENOB of the charge-domain MAC output. Device-level PV makes the ENOB vary from 6.49 bits down to a worst case of 5.33 bits (μ = 5.93, σ = 0.211 over 200 samples), a ~20% variation. Since low-precision neural network inference typically needs > 5–6 bits, this calls for tighter process control or PV-aware design.



Summary

  • PINN Compact Model: A 6-32-32-1 MLP trained on sparse 3-corner TCAD data, with ReLU-based physics losses enforcing monotone C-V behavior and correct εHZO, tHZO, Wov scaling trends.
  • Accuracy: R2 improved from 0.67 (MLP) to 0.96 (PINN) on an unseen process corner, with no unphysical ripples.
  • SPICE-Ready: Monotone, smooth C-V predictions avoid convergence failures in large-array circuit simulation.
  • Reliability Insight: PV causes ~20% ENOB variation in a 128×128 nvCAP crossbar, highlighting the need for PV-aware design.


Figures in this post: © 2026 IEEE. Reprinted, with permission, from G. Jeong, J. Kwak, M. Vadlamani, J. Lee, and S. Yu, “Physics-Informed Neural Network-Assisted Compact Modeling for Process Variation in Non-volatile Capacitive Crossbar Arrays,” IEEE International Reliability Physics Symposium (IRPS), 2026. IEEE Xplore
entry.summary: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) compact model for process variation in ferroelectric nvCAP crossbar arrays, enforcing monotone C-V and process trends with ReLU-based physics losses. Presented at IRPS 2026.

entry.title: Accelerating TCAD: AI Surrogate Modeling with PINO using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo Framework

link.title: Accelerating TCAD: AI Surrogate Modeling with PINO using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo Framework

entry.content:
Tutorial Video


Paper (ICMC 2026): Physics-informed AI Accelerated Retention Analysis of Ferroelectric Vertical NAND: From Day-Scale TCAD to Second-Scale Surrogate Model (arXiv:2603.06881)
Demo Code: github.com/gyulab/PINO-for-Semiconductor
Tutorial Slides: AI-Surrogate-modeling-tutorial.pdf

This work is a collaboration between Georgia Tech, Samsung Electronics, and NVIDIA, and was presented at ICMC (International Compact Modeling Conference) 2026! Note) We are preparing for the journal extension, stay tuned for updates!

Motivation: TCAD Bottleneck for Fe-VNAND Retention Analysis

    Ferroelectric FET (FeFET)-based vertical NAND (Fe-VNAND) is a promising candidate to overcome the Z-scaling limitations of 3D NAND with lower programming voltages. However, its data retention is hindered by a complex, time-dependent interplay between ferroelectric depolarization and charge detrapping at the dielectric interfaces. Optimizing the gate stack against these effects requires exploring a huge design space—geometry, temperature, and retention time.

    Conventional Technology Computer-Aided Design (TCAD) is accurate but computationally prohibitive: a single rigorous simulation sweeping temperature and time can take over 24 hours, and the cost scales linearly with every additional variable. To solve this, we developed a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO)-based AI surrogate model on the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework that predicts 2D physics maps, ID-VG curves, and Vth retention loss with near-TCAD accuracy in seconds.



Device and TCAD Training Data

    We study a single FeFET with an interlayer-engineered gate stack, where a Tunnel Dielectric Layer (TDL) is inserted between ferroelectric layers (HZO/TDL/HZO). During erase, charges accumulate at the HZO/TDL interface via Fowler-Nordheim tunneling and counteract the depolarization field. During retention, these screening charges detrap, which exacerbates the depolarization field and accelerates polarization loss.

    Training data were generated with Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD (ferroelectric Preisach model + FN tunneling, retention up to 104 s) by sweeping three inputs, giving only 120 TCAD sweeps in total:

Input Sweep Parameter Values
HZO Thickness {5, 6, 7, 8, 9} nm
Temperature {300, 358, 400, 473} K
Retention Time {0, 1e0, 1e1, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4} s


For each condition, we extract the ID-VG curve and internal 2D physics maps: electrostatic potential, polarization, and trapped electron/hole densities from the gate stack (HZO/TDL/HZO), and the current density from the entire device to capture channel conductance changes.



Methodology: Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO)

    Our model is not a “black box.” Instead of directly mapping scalar inputs to ID-VG curves, it first predicts intermediate physics maps, which makes the surrogate a physically interpretable digital twin and acts as a physical regularizer for the downstream readout.

Architecture


The pipeline consists of three phases:

  • Phase 1 – Input Embedding: Scalar device inputs (tHZO, T, log(τ)) are embedded into an input tensor.
  • Phase 2 – PINO Physics Surrogate: A Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) backbone performs global convolutions in the Fourier domain and maps the inputs to resolution-invariant 2D physics fields (J, Qe,h, V, P) on a 256×256 grid. To avoid overfitting the sparse dataset, the FNO is strictly regularized: 4 Fourier layers, modes = 12, latent width = 32.
  • Phase 3 – IV-Net Readout: A shallow CNN map encoder extracts features from the physics maps, while the original scalar inputs bypass the surrogate through a parallel MLP (scalar context injection). The two are fused to predict the final ID-VG curve. This residual path preserves global thermodynamic context (e.g., bake temperature) that cannot be extracted from purely electrostatic 2D maps.

Physics-Informed Loss Function

The key difference between a purely data-driven FNO and a PINO is the dual-loss objective:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{data} + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}_{physics} $$


where \(\mathcal{L}_{data}\) is the L2 error against TCAD ground truth, and \(\mathcal{L}_{physics}\) consists of two components:

  1. Poisson Residual: enforces that the predicted potential \(\phi\), charge density \(\rho\), and ferroelectric polarization \(P\) obey electrostatics.
$$ \mathcal{L}_{Poisson} = \nabla \cdot (\varepsilon \nabla \phi) + (\rho - \nabla \cdot P) $$
  1. Monotonicity Constraint: enforces the monotonic decay of remnant polarization and trapped charge over retention time, penalizing unphysical glitches or oscillations.
$$ \mathcal{L}_{mono} = ReLU\left(\frac{\partial |P_r|}{\partial \tau}\right) + ReLU\left(\frac{\partial |Q_{it}|}{\partial \tau}\right) $$


This physics-informed loss constrains the hypothesis space when training data are sparse, which is exactly the regime of expensive semiconductor simulations.



Results

1. Reconstruction Accuracy of 2D Physics Maps

    Validated against TCAD, the trained PINO reconstructs 2D profiles of electrostatic potential, trapped charge, and current density with a relative error of ~0.1%.



2. ID-VG Prediction and Retention Analysis

  • Vth Accuracy: R2 > 0.998 for Vth (at ID = 100 nA) over all 120 sweep conditions.
  • Unseen Temperature: The model produces physically consistent ΔVth retention curves at an unseen 350 K, lying between the 300 K and 400 K TCAD baselines.
  • Physics vs. Data-Driven: The purely data-driven FNO overfits the sparse dataset and shows unstable ripples across the transfer curve, while the PINO predicts a smooth ID-VG response, improving RMSE by > 40% (0.080 → 0.047).

3. Computational Efficiency

Metric TCAD AI Surrogate
Single sweep 30 min ~0.1 s (real-time)
Full sweep 60 hrs ~10 s
DSE coverage Discrete (prone to blind spots) Continuous (mesh-free interpolation)
Cost of optimization Prohibitive Minimal


(TCAD: Intel Xeon Platinum 8470N 52-core CPU, AI surrogate: NVIDIA Titan RTX 24 GB GPU)

    A full retention sweep goes from 60 hours to ~10 seconds, a speedup of four orders of magnitude (> 10,000×).



Open-Source Demo: PINO for Semiconductor

    To make the workflow reproducible, we released a demo repository, PINO-for-Semiconductor, that applies the same NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo-based FNO/PINO pipeline to 3D SONOS NAND flash devices. Watch the tutorial video at the top of this post for a walkthrough.

PINO-for-Semiconductor/
├── code/
│   ├── train_fno_model_sonos.py    # Standard FNO, MSE loss (data-driven only)
│   ├── train_pino_model_sonos.py   # PINO with Poisson residual loss
│   ├── inference_time_sweep.py     # Time-evolution animation of defect charge density
│   └── inference_pino_time.py      # PINO time-sweep inference
├── docs/
│   └── AI-Surrogate-modeling-tutorial.pdf
└── results/                        # FNO vs. PINO visualizations (below)

In train_pino_model_sonos.py, the Poisson equation \(\varepsilon \nabla^2 \phi + \rho = 0\) is implemented as a custom PhysicsNeMo Node, and its residual is driven to zero alongside the data loss. The training data (AMAT Ginestra simulations) are not included due to EULA/NDA restrictions.

FNO (Data-Driven): Defect Charge Density


PINO (Physics-Informed): Predicted Potential from Charge Density




Preliminary Proof-of-Concept

    Before the ICMC paper, we explored the framework on other configurations.

Design Space Exploration (Interpolation): Trained on 5, 7, and 9 nm HZO thicknesses, the model was queried for an unseen 8 nm device and predicted a max E-field of ~8.4 MV/cm, matching the verification TCAD simulation (30 min in TCAD vs. < 1 ms in AI).

AOS Channel String Array FeNAND: On a string array with amorphous oxide semiconductor (AOS) channels and Source/Gate/Drain regions, the AI reconstructed 2D current density maps with <1% reconstruction error, showing the model can handle complex boundaries and material interfaces needed for array-level modeling.



Summary and Future Work

    We developed a physics-informed AI surrogate model that faithfully accelerates Fe-VNAND retention analysis:

  • Efficiency: Trained on only 120 TCAD sweeps, with strict regularization to generalize to unseen temporal, thermal, and geometric regimes.
  • Speed: > 10,000× speedup (60 hrs → ~10 s for a full retention sweep), enabling continuous design space exploration.
  • Physics: Governed by Poisson’s equation and monotonicity constraints, eliminating unphysical artifacts and improving RMSE by > 40% over a data-driven FNO.
  • Compact Modeling: Serves as a physics-consistent data engine for compact model parameter extraction and LUT generation for reliability-aware SPICE simulation.

    Next, we are extending this work to full-scale 3D Fe-VNAND string arrays in a journal version. Stay tuned!
entry.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) surrogate for Ferroelectric Vertical NAND retention analysis on NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo: from day-scale TCAD to second-scale inference (>10,000x speedup). Presented at ICMC 2026, with an open-source demo and tutorial video.

entry.content:
Presentation Video


Official Example (IBM AIHWKit): examples/36_gpt2_on_wikitext.py
My Fork: github.com/gyulab/aihwkit (GPT-2, GPT-2 notebook, BERT noise analysis)

Update) The GPT-2 example I started in summer 2024 is now part of the official IBM AIHWKit examples as Example 36 (“This example was initiated by Gyujun Jeong”), released with AIHWKit 1.1.0 and later versions.

Motivation: Transformers on Analog In-Memory Computing

    Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) performs matrix-vector multiplications directly inside non-volatile memory crossbars, avoiding the data movement that dominates the energy of large neural networks. However, analog weights are noisy: programming noise, read noise, conductance drift, and limited ADC/DAC precision all perturb the computation.

    IBM Analog Hardware Acceleration Kit (AIHWKit) is an open-source PyTorch toolkit that simulates these non-idealities, so we can ask: how do modern transformer models behave on analog hardware, and which layers are most sensitive to noise? In this project, I explored two transformer families:

  1. GPT-2 (decoder): an end-to-end example for analog conversion, hardware-aware (HWA) fine-tuning, and text generation.
  2. BERT (encoder): a layer-by-layer noise sensitivity analysis on question answering.



Part 1. GPT-2 on AIHWKit

Model & Dataset

  • Model: DistilGPT2 (88.2M parameters), the smallest GPT-2 variant, for demonstration.
  • Dataset: wikitext-2-raw-v1 (~18 MB on disk).
  • Workflow: load the pre-trained model from Hugging Face → convert it to analog with convert_to_analog() → HWA fine-tuning → evaluate perplexity at different weight noise levels and inference times (drift), logged to TensorBoard.

Analog Layers

    After convert_to_analog(), the LM head (768 → 50257) becomes an AnalogLinear layer mapped onto two simulated crossbar tiles. In this demonstration, the GPT-2 blocks use Hugging Face Conv1D modules (attention c_attn/c_proj, MLP c_fc/c_proj), which were not replaced by the converter, so they stay digital along with the embeddings and LayerNorms.


Results



Model Validation Loss Perplexity (PPL)
Digital (reference, Intel/distilgpt2-wikitext2) 3.326 27.8
Analog, HWA fine-tuned (AIHWKit) 4.059 57.9


    The analog model still generates coherent text from a prompt, showing that the full pipeline (conversion → HWA training → generation) works end-to-end:

  • Input: “Once upon a time”
  • Output: “Once upon a time of war, the German army was able to defeat the German army in the Battle of the Rhine”


    I opened a pull request to IBM/AIHWKit (#664). The example was later integrated by the maintainers into the official repository as Example 36.



Part 2. BERT Noise Analysis on SQuAD

Setup

  • Task: SQuAD v1.1 (100k+ question-answer pairs). BERT takes [CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP] and predicts start/end logits of the answer span.
  • Metrics: F1 score (token overlap between predicted and ground-truth spans) and Exact Match (EM).
  • Analog configuration: PCM-like noise model, 512×512 tiles, 256-level DAC/ADC resolution, output noise, and global drift compensation.
  • Method: For each layer, one at a time, inject Gaussian weight noise (mean = 0, std = 0.1) and re-evaluate F1/EM. This isolates how much each layer contributes to the accuracy loss.



Baseline

    Without additional noise, the analog BERT achieves F1 ≈ 88 and EM ≈ 81, stable over drift times up to 106 s. This is the reference for the layer-wise analysis.


Layer-wise Sensitivity

Layer Group F1 / EM under noise Observation
Embeddings (word, position, token type) F1 0.59–4.19, EM < 1 Most vulnerable: noise corrupts the input representation itself
Attention (query/key/value) F1 86.75–87.47, EM 78.67–79.67 Robust: attention tolerates noise to a certain extent
Intermediate / output dense Mostly ~87, worst F1 77.13, EM 63.69 Complex output dense layers can be highly sensitive
LayerNorm F1 ~87, EM ~79 Strong resistance; normalization stabilizes small perturbations
QA outputs F1 ~87, EM ~79 Robust: directly reads the contextualized embeddings




    Noise propagation: Noise injected in earlier layers propagates and can be amplified downstream. For example, the same output dense tile gives F1 87.23 in encoder layer 0 but drops to F1 77.13 in layer 3.


Why Are Some Layers Vulnerable?

Hypothesis 1, Weight magnitude: “Heavier weights dominate, so they are more noise-sensitive.” I correlated the mean and std of each tile’s weights with its F1 score. The correlation coefficients were only −0.005 (mean) and 0.090 (std), so weight magnitude is not the explanation.


Hypothesis 2, Distribution spread: Comparing the vulnerable layer (output.dense ... array.3.0, F1 77.13) with an average layer (F1 88.24), the vulnerable layer shows a wider weight distribution and less consistent neuron activations. This higher variability makes it less able to generalize under perturbation, which likely explains its lower F1.




Summary

  • GPT-2 on AIHWKit: Built an end-to-end analog GPT-2 example (conversion, HWA fine-tuning, drift-aware evaluation, text generation), now included in the official IBM AIHWKit as Example 36.
  • Layer importance: In BERT, the first layers (embeddings) and complex final transformations (output dense) are the most critical, since they handle the initial encoding of raw input and the final prediction.
  • Layer functionality: Layers with complex transformations and wider weight/activation distributions are more susceptible to analog noise, while attention, LayerNorm, and QA outputs are comparatively robust.
  • Takeaway for hardware design: Not all layers need the same analog precision. Keeping sensitive layers (e.g., embeddings) digital or giving them more robust mapping is a practical path for transformer inference on AIMC.


Slides: BERT Noise Analysis using AIHWKit (July 18, 2024)

Slides: GPT-2 Example Implementation (June 25, 2024)

entry.title: LoRa/CSS: Overview, Demodulation and Decoding
entry.content:
Note: Source code details have been omitted for security reasons.


Overview of LoRa


    LoRa (Long Range) is a proprietary wireless communication technology that is used for long-range communication and low-power, low-data-rate applications. LoRa is based on the spread spectrum technique and uses a frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) approach to transmit data over long distances.



LoRa Modulation


  • Employs CSS(Chirp Spread Spectrum modulation)
         Chirp: Signals with constantly increasing(Up-) or decreasing(Down-) frequency
         Usually up-chirp utilized on LoRa Mod

  • Key parameter: Spreading Factor (SF)
    SF(Spreading Factor): Bits per symbol (5<SF<13)
    The SF satisfies SF = B · T , where B is bandwidth and T is chirp period. There are at most SF cyclically shifted up-chirp symbols given a specific SF. An up-chirp can be represented as the following formula:

$$ chirp(t; f0) = Aexp[j2πf0+ \frac{B}{2T} t)t] $$


The higher the SF, the longer the time on air, resulting in higher energy per bit.

    A LoRa symbol is a cyclic shift in frequency that is controlled by chirping rates represented with a spreading factor (SF), which determines the symbol’s spreading over time. A normalized up-chirp LoRa signal is expressed as follows:

$$ s(t) = \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} \sqrt{SF} \exp\left(j2\pi[\gamma(m) + \beta t/2\right)_{mod B} - \frac{B}{2}]t. $$


    The frequency offset, γ(m), and chirp slope, β, are obtained from m, the symbol being modulated, B, the transmission bandwidth, and Ts, the symbol time. The SF has a range of SF ∈ {6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12}, while the bandwidth B ∈ {125, 250, 500} kHz. The chirp rate has a slope of fhigh − flow = B/Ts.


    An example of a LoRa chirp is shown in the above figure, which depicts the spectrogram of a LoRa symbol, highlighting the cyclic frequency shift. Each symbol represents M = 2^SF bits according to the LoRa modulation convention.
    With these knowledges, we can make chirp generator program for given domain as follows:


LoRa Waveform Structure



  • Preamble -> (Sync) -> SFD -> (Header) -> Data
        Preamble: Sync detection, i.e., Start point of the signal
        Sync: Frame sync, utilized after demodulation - bit analysis
        SFD(Start Frame Delimiter): Identifier, i.e., Delimiter, Down-chirp
        Data: CSS-Modulated data, varying start frequency

LoRa Demodulation


    Typically, LoRa detection is achieved in two steps: (i) first, the signal is de-chirped, then (ii) typical FSK demodulation is applied. De-chirping is achieved by mixing the received LoRa symbol with an inverted chirp (down-chirp) with no frequency offset. Since the demodulator has no prior knowledge of the transmit symbols, the de-chirping signal utilizes γ(0) = −B/2. Hence, the resulting signal is given as follows:

$$ s(t) = \sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}} \sqrt{SF} \exp\left(j2\pi mδ_f t\right){} $$


which is a typical M-ary FSK signal. Each symbol is now represented with a frequency shift of mδf, where δf is the bandwidth divided by the number of steps. In LoRa, it happens that this value is equivalent to the symbol rate as follows, δf = 1/T.
    Now that the symbol is modulated using FSK, we can use conventional FSK demodulation methods to detect the symbol. Here, we utilized Non-coherent detection, attained by using energy detection in the frequency domain, where the maximum PSD peak location indicates the extracted symbol, formulated as follows:

$$ \hat{m}_{n-coh} = \frac{1}{δ_f}argmax[[R(f)] − 0.5] $$


where R(f) is implemented as the fast Fourier transform (FFT) of the FSK signal, R(f) = FFT{r(t)}.
    Using this approach, we can easily implement a LoRaWan-like demodulator by following these simple snippet.

    To de-chirp the signal, we start by cross-correlating it with a reference downchirp. This is done using np.convolve with mode 'valid'. The index where the maximum correlation is achieved corresponds to the timing of the received data, which we obtain using data_index = argmax(crosscorr_result). We then perform an FFT on each dechirped data and proceed with symbol-to-bit mapping as described earlier. Using multiprocessing, as discussed in earlier post, can accelerate the iterative loop.

LoRa Decoding


The LoRa receiver performs synchronization, frequency-offset estimation, and compensation prior to demodulation. Gray coding, de-interleaving, de-whitening, and Hamming decoding are carried out to recover the information as described in the figure above. In this post, we will discuss the concept of those decoding processes in general and how they apply to the LoRa decoding process.

Gray coding


A gray coding is a mapping between a symbol in any numeric representation to a binary sequence. The particularity of the obtained binary sequence is that adjacent symbols in the original representation only differ by one bit in the gray representation. This property of a gray codes make them very useful in many wireless communication modulations where it is more likely to misinterpret a symbol by an adjacent one than another random one. It is noteworthy that in the case of CSS modulation it is not the white noise that causes this misinterpretation between adjacent symbols but the carrier and sampling frequency offset. In the case of LoRa, the symbols can be seen as integers between 0 and 2^SF − 1 and by making usage of gray coding to map them to binary strings, we increase the performance of the forward error correction mechanisms capable of correcting one erroneous bit in a codeword.

Unfortunately, it is possible to create different binary string sequences respecting the conditions to be considered as a gray code. Furthermore it is just a mapping between decimal numbers and binary string, meaning that once we have found a sequence of 2^SF binary string differing by only one bit, we can still define any of them to by mapped to 0. Finally the direction of mapping of the following symbol can also be chosen freely. This leads to 2 ∗ 2^SF possibilities for every possible gray sequence. The method used in was a brute force approach, which found out that the method of the figure 2.4 is used.


Important Note: The standard gray code being used is given by Cn = Bn XOR (Bn » 1) where Bn is the left MSB binary representation of n. On top of the mapping using this gray code, a shift of -1 is used, i.e., v = (v0 − 1) XOR ((v0 − 1) » 1).

  • In MATLAB
    Read the following document to understand the bin2gray function.

  • In Python

We can note that the gray coding doesn’t occur in the conventional order but in reverse which still holds the property that one adjacent symbol mistake leads only to one bit being wrong. The figure 2.5 present the binary values obtained after gray encoding of the received LoRa symbols line by line. The white and black square are respectively ones and zeros.

Interleaving and De-interleaving


    Interleaving is a technique used to improve the performance of error correction codes by breaking the correlation between errors caused by noise or fading. It works by spreading the bits of a codeword across multiple symbols, so that if a symbol is corrupted, the errors will be distributed across multiple codewords rather than concentrated in one. This increases the effectiveness of the error correction code, but also increases the latency of the communication. Interleaving can also be used to improve the robustness of data transmitted over a noisy channel.

    For instance, LoRa signal applies diagonal interleaving instead of conventional row-line interleaving. The Figure (a) shows the column-major order row-line interleaving of eight symbols. For row-line interleaving, the LSBs (bi,1) of the eight symbols are assembled into a byte. From Section 3 we know that the LSBs of a symbol are more fragile than the most signiicant bits (MSBs) of the symbol. From the perspective of FEC, it is a bad design to group fragile bits together. Figure 9(b) shows diagonal interleaving used in LoRa. Diagonal interleaving distributes the fragile LSBs into diferent bytes and is more robust. We then manipulate the transmitted packets to derive the detailed diagonal mapping.

    As an example, we send packets with SF = 8 and CR = 4/8 in implicit header mode. Thus, the interleaving block is an 8 × 8 block as shown in Figure 9(b). First, we assume the FEC used in CR = 4/8 is the standard (7,4) Hamming code with one bit extension. Therefore, after Gray coding and Whitening, the codeword for nibble 0000 is 00000000, and the codeword for 1111 is 11111111. Suppose the sending bytes are all zeros except that the fourth byte is 0x0F, we observe b11 = b22 = · · · = b88 = 1 in Figure 9(b). Therefore the main diagonal represents the fourth byte 0x0F. The one bin shift problem mentioned in Gray coding relects here that we cannot always get eight ones in a block if we directly apply the standard Gray coding. Shifting the mapping by one solves this problem and perfectly matches our following decoding process. By changing the all-1 data bits in the transmitted packet, we can derive the entire mapping for interleaving as shown in Figure9(b). For other parameters, the deinterleaving process is similar. The only diference is that the block size becomes 4/CR × SF.


Important Note: From these patterns, we can finally extract the following general interleaving formula: I(i,j) = D(j,(i−(j+1)%SF))where I is the interleaved matrix and D the deinterleaved one.


  • Simple snippet in cpp code


Whitening and De-whitening (De-randomizing)


    Whitening (Randomizing) is a technique that uses XORing bits with a pseudo-random sequence to remove the DC-bias from transmitted data. Unlike Manchester coding, it maintains the same data rate, but does not guarantee the removal of DC-bias, only a high probability of doing so.

    LoRa chip datasheet (Semtech. Data Sheet SX1276/77/78/79, Rev. 7, 2020) mentions that the whitening sequence in FSK mode is generated by a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR). We guess that there also exists a LFSR generating the whitening sequence for LoRa mode. We apply Berlekamp-Massey algorithm on the whitening sequences of the two decoding orders to obtain the corresponding LFSR.


Important Note: The whitening is based around the 9-bit LFSR polynomial x^9+x^5+1. With this structure, the least significant bit (LSB) at the output of the LFSR is XORed with the most significant bit (MSB) of the data.


  • Simple snippet

Multiprocessing and Multithreading


Multithreading and multiprocessing are techniques used to improve the performance of code by allowing multiple tasks to be executed simultaneously.

Multithreading is a technique where multiple threads of execution are created within a single process. Each thread runs independently, allowing multiple tasks to be performed concurrently. In a multithreaded program, each thread shares the same memory space and resources, but each thread has its own stack and set of registers. Multithreading is often used in programs that perform I/O or other blocking operations, where one thread can wait for I/O to complete while another thread performs computation.

Multiprocessing, on the other hand, is a technique where multiple processes are created, each with its own memory space and resources. Each process runs independently, allowing multiple tasks to be performed concurrently. Multiprocessing is often used in programs that perform CPU-intensive tasks, such as image or video processing, where multiple cores or processors can be utilized to improve performance.

The key difference between multithreading and multiprocessing is that multithreading allows multiple threads to execute within the same process, while multiprocessing allows multiple processes to execute concurrently.

Both techniques can improve code performance by leveraging the power of modern CPUs, which typically have multiple cores or processors. By dividing tasks among multiple threads or processes, the workload can be distributed across multiple cores or processors, resulting in faster execution times. However, the choice of whether to use multithreading or multiprocessing depends on the nature of the task being performed and the resources available. In general, multithreading is preferred for tasks that involve I/O or other blocking operations, while multiprocessing is preferred for tasks that are CPU-intensive.

Suppose we need to read and process a signal file that has a large data size. Reading and processing the signal would take a significant amount of time. To improve the performance, we can use multithreading for the signal readout sequence and multiprocessing for the signal processing sequence. Here is the code for the signal readout and processing, including fixed-point conversion:

Since reading the file is an I/O bound operation, let’s apply multithreading to the readout part now:

To implement multithreading for the readoutSignal function, we can split the input file into multiple parts and read each part in a separate thread. In this implementation, the num_threads parameter specifies the number of threads to use. The file_size variable is calculated using the os.path.getsize function, and the chunk_size is calculated based on the file size and the number of threads. The chunks variable is a list of file positions, each representing the start of a chunk.

We create a thread for each chunk using the threading.Thread constructor and pass the read_chunk function as the target. The args parameter is used to pass the start and end file positions to the function. We start each thread with the start() method. After starting all threads, we wait for them to complete using the join() method. Once all threads have completed, we concatenate all the results in the results list and return the final read input data as a single array.

Now, let’s apply multiprocessing to the signal processing part, specifically the fixed-point conversion, since file processing is a CPU-bound operation:

This code defines a function called multiprocessFixedtoFloat that takes in an input_data array as an argument. The goal of this function is to convert the fixed-point numbers in input_data to floating-point numbers using multiple processes to speed up the computation. The first line of the function uses the multiprocessing.cpu_count() function to get the number of available CPUs on the system, and then subtracts 1 to leave one CPU available for other tasks. This value is stored in the num_cpu variable. Each chunk is created by slicing the input_data array into a piece of length pool_length. The chunks are stored in the chunks list. The multiprocessing.Pool() function is then used to create a pool of worker processes, with the number of processes equal to num_cpu. The pool.map() function is used to apply the convertFixedPoint function to each chunk of input_data in parallel. The pool_results variable is assigned the result of the pool.map() function, which is a list of arrays of floating-point numbers. The pool.close() function is then called to close the pool of worker processes.





[References]

  1. Liando, Jansen & Jg, Amalinda & Tengourtius, Agustinus & Li, Mo. (2019). Known and Unknown Facts of LoRa: Experiences from a Large-scale Measurement Study. ACM Transactions on Sensor Networks. 15. 1-35. 10.1145/3293534.
  2. Tapparel Joachim, Complete Reverse Engineering of LoRa PHY: https://www.epfl.ch/labs/tcl/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Reverse_Eng_Report.pdf
  3. https://lora.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
  4. Modulation, 2015. LoRa Modulation Basics, Rev.2., https://www.semtech.com/uploards/documents/an1200.22.pdf
  5. Kosta Dakic et al, LoRa Signal Demodulation Using Deep Learning, a Time-Domain Approach
  6. https://www.rfwireless-world.com/Tutorials/LoRaWAN-MAC-layer-inside.html
  7. Zhenqiang Xu, Pengjin Xie, Shuai Tong, and Jiliang Wang. 2022. From Demodulation to Decoding: Towards Complete LoRa PHY Understanding and Implementation. ACM Trans. Sen. Netw. Just Accepted (July 2022). https://doi.org/10.1145/3546869
  8. Ghanaatian, R., Afisiadis, O., Cotting, M., & Burg, A. (2019). Lora Digital Receiver Analysis and Implementation. ICASSP 2019 - 2019 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). doi:10.1109/icassp.2019.8683504

entry.title: GUI development with PyQT
entry.content:
PyQt is one of the most popular Python bindings for the Qt cross-platform C++ framework. Let us make a simple GUI to make a signal demodulator.


    This is an example of the PyQT designer window. Select and create a MainWindow. There are various widgets on the left, object lists on the top right, various properties of the selected object in the center right, and signal/slot editing windows on the bottom right.

    Now imagine the UI you want to create. Suppose you insert the file you want to demodulate, and you create an automatic processing program that generates a demodulated bit file.

    Adjust the size of the main window appropriately, and drag and place the necessary widgets from the left widget box. Add line edit where the I/O file name will be entered, push button to be an execution button such as file search, etc.

    Various objects would have been added to the upper right object inspector. It is recommended to change the object name so that it is easy to check later. (e.g., buttobOK, inputFileName, etc.)

    In the object inspector or center window, you can use the property editor in the center right by clicking on the desired object. In Designer, it is desirable to change only the appearance, such as size, and programmatic processing is handled in the main.py Python code.

    The signal/slot editor at the lower right deals with the signal of qt. When a signal (e.g., clicked()) of a specific object is connected to a slot (e.g., closed())), the signal executes an action corresponding to the slot when the signal is detected.

    Once you have created the UI shell with Designer, save and exit. After that, turn on the terminal on the path where the saved ui file is located and run the following command:

pyuic4 sample.ui -o ui.py -x

    It is a command that makes the UI file an importable Python script. A file is created as the name after -o, and if you insert the -x factor, it is created in a form that allows independent execution. Let’s run the file on Python and check it out.

    Now that we’ve created the UI, it’s time to write the main script. Depending on the size of the program, the script structure is written as desired, but the basic framework is as follows:


  • Class declaration
        If you look at ui.py generated by pyuic4, a class will be created as the name specified in the above designator: classUi_sample(object). It was created under the name UI. Later QtGui.We created a custom class called MainWindowWithEvent, which is a prototype of QMainWindow. This is to use the event. There are various events in Qt. It is a method that uses the most common keyPress Event, although there are various types such as window resize and mouse click. There are various values defined in QtCore.Qt, so refer to documentation.


  • Signals and Slots 
QtCore.Qobject.connect(UI.quitButton, QtCore.SIGNAL('clicked()'),quit)

    It is the most common signal-slot usage. Object called TryButton in UI (QtGui).When QPushButton) is clicked, process() is executed. There are various methods of using a custom slot.


  • Property usage
    For instance, QPushButton, commonly used in the GUI, has various properties and methods.
    UI.buttonA.setDisabled(True)

Disable the corresponding button. It can be enabled with setEnabled.

UI.buttonB.setChecked(True)

The corresponding button becomes clicked. If you insert False, it will not be clicked.

UI.buttonC.isChecked(True)

Returns a boolean value indicating whether it is a clicked state.

UI.buttonD.setText(str)

Show the value in str on the button.



    Now let’s make a GUI for signal demodulation in-depth.


    When the python code is executed on terminal, the demodulator GUI as follows is executed.

  2. https://wikidocs.net/35478
